title: NRI Tax Rules on Money Gifted to Hindu Undivided Families Explained
excerpt: Gifts from members are tax-free for the HUF, but clubbing provisions can push the income back onto the donor's tax return — here's what NRIs need to know.
body:
• Money gifted by an NRI to a Hindu Undivided Family is generally not taxable in the HUF's hands if the NRI is a member — but income earned from that gift gets clubbed with the donor's income under Section 64(2).
  • Gifts from non-members exceeding ₹50,000 in a financial year are taxable for the HUF under Section 56(2)(x) of the Income Tax Act.
  • NRIs managing HUF accounts should route transactions through NRO accounts and maintain gift deeds to withstand scrutiny by Indian tax authorities.
  • The clubbing provision applies only to income from the original gifted asset — reinvested income from that earnings stream is not clubbed and stays with the HUF.

For Non-Resident Indians managing family finances across borders, the Hindu Undivided Family remains one of the most misunderstood structures in Indian tax law. A recent Livemint advisory addressed a common question: what happens when an NRI gifts money to an HUF, and how should such transactions be handled to stay compliant with Indian income tax rules?

How Gifts to HUF Are Taxed

Under Section 56(2)(x) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, gifts received by an HUF from its members — known as relatives of the HUF under tax law — are fully exempt from tax, regardless of the amount. A member of the HUF is treated as a relative of the HUF, so there is no tax liability when the HUF receives money from a coparcener or other member, according to tax expert Balwant Jain writing in Livemint.

The exemption applies whether the gift is in cash, immovable property, or movable assets like shares and securities. If an NRI father gifts ₹10 lakh to his HUF, for example, the amount is entirely tax-free in the HUF's hands.

Gifts from non-relatives — anyone who is not a member of the HUF — follow different rules. Only up to ₹50,000 in aggregate gifts from non-relatives is exempt in a financial year. Any amount above that threshold is taxable as "income from other sources" in the hands of the HUF, as detailed by Motilal Oswal's tax guidance.

The Clubbing Trap

The real complexity lies in what happens after the gift. When a member gifts self-acquired property or money to the HUF, the income generated from that gift is clubbed back with the donor's income under Section 64(2) of the Income Tax Act. This means the HUF technically holds the asset, but any rental income, interest, or dividends it earns goes onto the donor's personal tax return.

According to TaxGuru, the clubbing provision continues to apply until the HUF's assets are fully partitioned. If an NRI Karta (head of the HUF) transfers money from his personal account to the HUF and the HUF invests it in fixed deposits, the interest income would be added to the Karta's taxable income — not the HUF's.

"Though the initial income is clubbed in the hands of the person who has given the gift, income from income in future years is not to be clubbed."

— TaxGuru advisory on HUF gift provisions

This distinction matters. If the HUF reinvests the interest income it earned (the "income from income"), that second-generation return is not subject to clubbing and remains taxable in the HUF's hands. This creates a legitimate, if slow, path to building HUF corpus over time.

NRO Accounts and Documentation

NRIs sending money to an HUF in India should use Non-Resident Ordinary (NRO) accounts for these transactions. If aggregate remittances exceed ₹10 lakh in a financial year, tax collection at source (TCS) provisions apply at 20% on the amount exceeding that threshold, according to chartered accountant Harshal Bhuta writing in Livemint. The TCS collected can be claimed as credit when filing Indian income tax returns.

For remittances, the authorized dealer bank may require a chartered accountant's certificate in Form 15CB to process the transfer. Proper documentation is critical — tax experts recommend executing a gift deed or gift declaration for every transfer to the HUF, even though the Income Tax Act does not technically mandate one.

Motilal Oswal's guidance outlines the documentation needed by gift type: bank transfer receipts and PAN details for cash gifts; registered gift deeds and valuation reports for immovable property; and allotment or transfer letters with valuation reports for shares and mutual funds.

What NRIs Frequently Get Wrong

Many NRIs create an HUF, transfer money from personal accounts, and start investing — expecting immediate tax benefits. According to Livemint, this often raises red flags with tax authorities, especially if the amounts are large or frequent. If a tax officer suspects the HUF is being used as a personal tax shelter, reassessments and penalties may follow.

Another common mistake: treating interest-free loans to the HUF as gifts. If money is structured as a loan, the assessing officer may invoke Section 60 provisions — treating it as transferring income without transferring the asset — and apply clubbing anyway, according to tax expert Balwant Jain.

Practical Steps for Diaspora Families

For NRI families considering HUF tax planning, the most effective approach is funding the HUF through gifts from relatives who are not coparceners. Gifts from a father or father-in-law to the HUF, for instance, are exempt and the income generated is not subject to clubbing, since the donor is not converting personal property into HUF property. This remains the "entirely legal and perfect way to create capital for your HUF," according to Livemint.

NRIs should consult a chartered accountant familiar with both FEMA regulations and HUF taxation before structuring any transfers — the intersection of cross-border compliance and domestic tax law creates pitfalls that generic tax advice often misses.
nri_angle: Directly addresses NRIs managing family finances in India through HUF structures — covers tax implications, documentation requirements, and common mistakes diaspora families make.
